b: Paul’s angriest letter. After he founded the churches of Galatia, other teachers arrived telling the Gentile converts that to belong fully to God’s people they must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses. Paul does not treat this as a side issue. To add anything to Christ as a condition of acceptance is, he says, a different gospel (1:6–9).

The letter moves in three stages. Chapters 1–2 defend Paul’s gospel and his authority, and end with the key statement of the whole letter (2:15–21). Chapters 3–4 argue from the Galatians’ own experience and from Scripture, especially Abraham, that God has always accepted people through faith. Chapters 5–6 show what freedom in Christ looks like: not a licence to sin, but life led by the Spirit and lived out in love.

The name goes back to Celtic peoples (Greek Galatai, the same word as ‘Gauls’) who moved from Europe into central Asia Minor in the third century BC. The geographer Strabo, writing around the time of Jesus, names their three tribes and their towns, including Ancyra — modern Ankara.

In 25 BC, when the last Galatian king, Amyntas, died, Augustus took his kingdom into the Roman empire as the province of Galatia (Cassius Dio 53.26). The province reached far south of the old tribal lands, taking in parts of Phrygia, Lycaonia and Pisidia. That brought in the cities Paul evangelised on his first journey: Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe (Acts 13–14).
So in Paul’s day ‘Galatia’ could mean two things: the old Celtic heartland in the north, or the whole Roman province. That double meaning is behind the debate in the next item.

hist.t: Which churches did Paul write to: North or South Galatia?
b: The North Galatian view says Paul wrote to churches in the old Celtic territory around Ancyra, Pessinus and Tavium. It takes ‘the region of Phrygia and Galatia’ (Acts 16:6; 18:23) to mean a visit to that northern region on Paul’s second journey, and usually dates the letter to the mid-50s AD, close to Romans, which covers similar ground.

The South Galatian view, championed by the archaeologist William Ramsay, says the readers were the churches of Acts 13–14. Its main arguments are these. Paul usually uses Roman provincial names (Achaia, Macedonia, Asia). Acts records churches in the south but never founds any in the north. And the Galatians evidently knew Barnabas (2:1, 9, 13), who travelled with Paul only on the first journey. This view allows an early date, possibly before the Jerusalem council of Acts 15 (around AD 48–49), which would explain why Paul never mentions the council’s ruling.

Where scholars stand: the New Bible Dictionary describes New Testament scholars as ‘almost evenly divided’, and the debate continues today. Nothing in the letter’s teaching depends on the answer; it affects only the date and how the letter fits with Acts.

hist.t: The southern cities in the ground
b: Pisidian Antioch was refounded by Augustus as a Roman colony in 25 BC. A University of Michigan expedition in 1924 uncovered a sanctuary of the imperial cult dedicated to Augustus, a monumental city gate, and about 200 more fragments of a stone copy of Augustus’s own account of his reign (the Res Gestae), displayed in a prominent public place. Paul preached in the synagogue of this very Roman city (Acts 13:14–50).

Lystra was also made a Roman colony by Augustus. Its site, a mound (Zoldera Höyük) near the village of Hatunsaray, was identified from a Latin altar inscription found in 1885 and from later finds, but the town itself has never been excavated. Surviving inscriptions show a considerable Latin-speaking settlement. Acts 14:11 notes that the crowd there spoke ‘in the Lycaonian language’. That fits what is known: Latin-speaking colonists were settled among a population that kept its own local culture and speech.

Why it matters: if the South Galatian view is right, Paul’s readers lived in cities where loyalty to Rome and the emperor was built into public life, as the Antioch sanctuary shows. Gentile converts who stopped honouring the gods and the emperor would have stood out.

1.t: Every other Pauline letter opens with thanksgiving. This one goes straight to astonishment, then to a double curse on anyone preaching another gospel. The stakes are not presented as secondary.
Paul's account of his own calling is given to establish that his gospel was not handed down through Jerusalem. The autobiography is an argument.

2.h: Paul opposes Peter to his face
2.t: Peter withdrew from eating with Gentiles when representatives from James arrived. Paul treats table fellowship as a gospel issue rather than a matter of preference, because what Peter's action implied was that Gentile believers were second class.

2.h: Justified by faith, not works of law
2.t: The doctrinal statement of the letter. Verse 20 — crucified with Christ, no longer I who live — is not mysticism but the logic of union with him.

3.t: Paul argues from their own experience of the Spirit, then from Abraham, who was counted righteous before the law existed and before he was circumcised. The chronology does the work.
Christ became a curse for us, quoting Deuteronomy on the man hanged on a tree. Substitution stated as directly as anywhere in Paul.
A statement about standing before God in Christ, and one with consequences the church has been slow to work out. It does not erase distinctions; it denies that they determine status.

4.t: In the fullness of time, God sent his Son; and because we are sons, he sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts crying Abba. Both sendings, and adoption as the result.

5.t: The thesis of the second half. Freedom is something to stand in rather than to celebrate abstractly.
The works of the flesh are mostly relational — hostility, strife, jealousy, factions — and so is the fruit of the Spirit. Note it is fruit singular, one cluster, not a menu of gifts.

6.t: Instruction for when a brother is caught in sin: restoration, by those who are spiritual, with gentleness, watching yourself. Then carry each other's burdens.
Paul's closing, in his own large handwriting. The cross is the only credential he will now claim.

1.ctx: Paul writes to churches he founded in the Roman province of Galatia, in what is now central Turkey. Teachers have since arrived insisting that Gentile converts must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses. Galatians is probably one of the earliest of Paul’s letters (see History & setting above).
1.mean: Paul opens by answering two charges before anyone has made them. First, his authority. He is an apostle ‘sent not from men nor by man’, sent directly by Jesus Christ and God the Father. His critics evidently said he was a second-hand apostle, dependent on Jerusalem. Second, his message. In one line he summarises the gospel: Christ ‘gave himself for our sins to rescue us from the present evil age’. That sentence already contains the argument of the letter. If Christ’s self-giving deals with our sins and rescues us, nothing needs to be added to it. ‘The present evil age’ is Jewish language for the world as it now is under sin, contrasted with the age to come; Paul says the rescue into that new age has already begun.
1.big: Both Paul’s authority and his gospel rest on what God has done in Christ, not on human credentials or human effort.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Galatians (Calvin Translation Society, 1854), CCEL

1.ctx: In every other letter Paul follows the greeting with thanks for his readers. Here he leaves the thanks out and goes straight to astonishment, which his first readers would have noticed at once.
1.mean: Paul is amazed ‘how quickly you are deserting the One who called you by the grace of Christ’, for ‘a different gospel’. He immediately corrects himself: it is not another gospel at all, only a distortion of the one gospel. Then, twice, he pronounces a curse (Greek anathema, something handed over to God for judgment) on anyone who preaches a gospel contrary to the one they received. That includes Paul himself, or even an angel. The point is that the message has authority, not the messenger. The teachers in Galatia probably did not deny Christ. They added to him: faith in Christ plus circumcision and the law. Paul’s verdict is that the addition changes the whole thing.
1.big: Adding a requirement to Christ as the condition of being accepted by God does not improve the gospel; it replaces it.

1.ctx: Paul’s opponents seem to have claimed that he watered down the gospel to please Gentiles, and that he had learned it second-hand from the Jerusalem apostles.
1.mean: Paul says he is not a people-pleaser; if he were, he would not be Christ’s servant. He received his gospel ‘by revelation from Jesus Christ’, meaning the risen Christ’s appearance to him on the Damascus road (Acts 9). He then gives evidence. He was the most zealous of persecutors, so no human argument converted him; God did. After his call he went to Arabia, not Jerusalem, and only three years later spent fifteen days with Cephas (Peter) and met James, the Lord’s brother. The Judean churches knew him only by report, and they ‘glorified God because of me’. Paul is not claiming the Jerusalem apostles disagreed with him. His point is that he did not get his gospel from them.
1.big: Paul’s gospel was not borrowed from anyone; it came from the risen Christ, and his changed life is the proof.
1.diff: Verse 15 says God ‘set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me by his grace’. Reformed interpreters see here God’s sovereign choosing in Paul’s own conversion: God acted before Paul could do anything. Others, Arminian interpreters among them, agree that the initiative was God’s, but note that the language echoes the prophetic calls of Jeremiah (1:5) and the Servant (Isaiah 49:1), so Paul is describing his calling to a task (preaching to the Gentiles, verse 16) rather than teaching how individuals come to be saved. The two readings can overlap. Where Paul went in ‘Arabia’ and why is unknown: possibly to preach in the Nabataean kingdom (compare 2 Corinthians 11:32), possibly for a period of reflection.

2.ctx: Fourteen years later (after his conversion or after his first visit; Paul does not say which), Paul goes up to Jerusalem with Barnabas and Titus. Titus is a Gentile believer who had not been circumcised, so he is a test case in person.
2.mean: Paul laid his gospel privately before the leaders. Some ‘false brothers’ tried to have Titus circumcised, but Paul did not give way ‘so that the truth of the gospel would remain with you’, and the leaders did not insist. James, Cephas and John, the recognised ‘pillars’, added nothing to Paul’s message. They saw that God had entrusted him with the gospel for the Gentiles as he had Peter for the Jews, and gave him the right hand of fellowship. Their one request, to remember the poor, was something Paul was already eager to do. So the very people the Galatian teachers appealed to had already accepted an uncircumcised Gentile believer as a full brother.
2.big: The leading apostles in Jerusalem recognised Paul’s gospel as the same gospel, with nothing added.
2.diff: Scholars differ over which visit in Acts this is. If it is the famine-relief visit of Acts 11:30, the letter may come before the Jerusalem council of Acts 15, which would explain why Paul never quotes the council’s decision. If it is the council visit itself, Paul is describing the private meetings behind the public decision. Both views are held by careful scholars, and neither affects the teaching.

2.ctx: Antioch in Syria, the third city of the empire and home of the first mixed church of Jews and Gentiles (Acts 11:19–26). Sharing a meal there meant full acceptance, and many devout Jews avoided eating with Gentiles because of the food laws and purity rules.
2.mean: Peter had been eating with Gentile believers. When ‘certain men came from James’, he drew back and separated himself ‘for fear of those in the circumcision group’. The other Jewish believers followed, even Barnabas. Peter had not changed his theology; Paul calls it ‘hypocrisy’, acting against what he knew to be true. But the effect was to divide the church into two tables. The unspoken message to Gentile Christians was that to be fully accepted they must become Jews. So Paul opposed Peter publicly, ‘to his face’, because they were ‘not walking in line with the truth of the gospel’: ‘If you, who are a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you compel the Gentiles to live like Jews?’ Paul treats who eats with whom as a gospel question. If acceptance rests on Christ alone, no believer can be made a second-class member.
2.big: How believers treat one another at the table is a gospel issue, because it shows whether acceptance rests on Christ alone.
2.diff: It is unclear whether Paul’s words to Peter end at verse 14 or run on to verse 21. Many commentators think verses 15–21 restate what Paul said at Antioch in a form aimed at the Galatians. The note on 2:15 treats them separately. Some early Christian writers were uncomfortable with two apostles in conflict and suggested the quarrel was staged for teaching purposes; Jerome took this view. Augustine argued against it in his letters to Jerome: Peter really was in the wrong, and Scripture does not report pretence as truth.

2.h: Justified by Faith, Not by Works of the Law
2.ctx: The heart of the letter, and one of the most important paragraphs Paul wrote. Here he states what was at stake at Antioch. Peter knew this, the Galatians had forgotten it, and the rest of the letter defends it. It closely parallels Romans 3:20–28.
2.mean:
The common ground (verse 15). Paul starts where Peter and every Jewish believer stood: ‘We who are Jews by birth and not Gentile “sinners”…’ The quotation marks matter. ‘Sinners’ was what Jews commonly called Gentiles, people outside God’s covenant and law. Paul is setting a trap.

The great reversal (verse 16). Even Jews with every advantage ‘know that a man is not justified by works of the law, but by faith in Jesus Christ’. To be justified is a law-court word: to be declared in the right before God, the judge. If the people who had the law still had to come to God by faith in Christ, then the law was never the way in, for them or for anyone. Paul says it three times in one verse and ends with an echo of Psalm 143:2: ‘by works of the law no one will be justified’. The reason, which Paul spells out in 3:10–12 and Romans 3:19–20, is that everyone has broken the law. The law can show what righteousness is and expose our sin, but it cannot make a sinner righteous. Jew and Gentile are on the same footing after all: both are sinners, both justified the same way.

The objection (verses 17–18). If seeking to be justified in Christ means Jews end up classed with Gentile ‘sinners’, ‘does that make Christ a minister of sin? Certainly not!’ Christ did not create the sin; he revealed what was already true. The real lawbreaking would be to rebuild the law as the ground of acceptance after tearing it down. That is exactly what Peter did by withdrawing from the table.

Death and new life (verses 19–20). ‘Through the law I died to the law, so that I might live to God.’ The law itself, by condemning Paul, brought him to the end of himself. In Christ he has died to it as a way of standing before God. ‘I have been crucified with Christ.’ Paul is united to Christ so closely that Christ’s death counts as his, and Christ now lives in him. His ordinary life is lived ‘by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself up for me’. This is personal faith in a person, not trust in a system.

The conclusion (verse 21). ‘If righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing.’ If our obedience could put us right with God, the cross would be unnecessary. So to add the law as a requirement is to say that Christ’s death was not enough.
2.big: No one is put right with God by keeping the law, because everyone has broken it; we are put right only through faith in Christ, who loved us and gave himself for us.
2.diff:
What are ‘works of the law’? The Reformers (Luther and Calvin) and many Reformed and evangelical scholars hold that the phrase means doing what the law of Moses requires, the moral law included, as a basis for acceptance. Calvin said the context ‘clearly proves that the moral law is also comprehended in these words’. He was answering earlier writers, including Origen and Jerome, who limited it to ceremonies such as circumcision and food laws. The ‘New Perspective on Paul’ (E. P. Sanders, James Dunn, N. T. Wright) stresses that the issue in Galatia was the law’s ‘boundary markers’ (circumcision, food laws, Sabbath), which separated Jews from Gentiles. Dunn himself says the phrase covers the whole law, viewed especially through those markers. Others, such as Thomas Schreiner, accept that circumcision and food laws were the issue in Galatia, but argue from 3:10, 5:3 and Romans 3:20 that the phrase means everything the law requires, so Paul’s reasoning applies to all the law’s demands.

‘Faith in Christ’ or ‘the faithfulness of Christ’? The Greek pistis Christou can mean either. Most translations, and scholars such as Bruce, Dunn and Schreiner, read ‘faith in Christ’, noting that the same verse says ‘we, too, have believed in Christ Jesus’. Richard Hays, J. Louis Martyn and Richard Longenecker argue for ‘the faithfulness of Christ’, meaning his obedience unto death. Both readings make Christ, not our law-keeping, the ground of justification.

What is justification? The Protestant traditions, Reformed, Lutheran and Arminian alike, agree that justification is God’s free verdict of acceptance received by faith, not earned. Reformed theology adds that Christ’s righteousness is counted (‘imputed’) to the believer (Westminster Confession 11.1). John Wesley described it as ‘pardon, the forgiveness of sins’. The Catholic Church teaches, from the Council of Trent, that justification is ‘not remission of sins merely, but also the sanctification and renewal of the inward man’, received first in baptism. Trent also teaches that nothing before justification, whether faith or works, earns it. The difference is over what justification is: a verdict, or a verdict together with an inner renewal.

hist.t: ‘Works of the law’ in the Dead Sea Scrolls
b: Until the 1990s, ‘works of the law’ was known almost only from Paul. Then a Dead Sea Scroll known as 4QMMT, preserved in six fragmentary copies from Qumran Cave 4 and probably composed in the mid-second century BC, became widely available. It is a letter from the community’s leaders listing more than twenty disputed points of law, mostly about temple purity, sacrifices and festivals. Its name comes from a phrase near the end, miqṣat ma‘aśe ha-Torah. Its editor, Elisha Qimron, translated it ‘some of the precepts of the Torah’; others, such as Martin Abegg, translate it ‘some of the works of the law’, Paul’s very phrase. The writers tell the reader that doing these things ‘will be reckoned to you as righteousness’.

This is the closest parallel to Paul’s phrase from his own century, and both sides of the modern debate use it. To some, it shows that ‘works of the law’ meant the specific rulings that marked out a group as faithful. To others, it shows that keeping the law’s requirements was linked with being counted righteous before God, which is exactly the link Paul denies. What is not disputed is that Paul’s phrase was real Jewish vocabulary in his day, not his own invention.

3.ctx: Paul turns from his own story to the Galatians’ experience. ‘Bewitched’ (Greek baskainō) is a word for casting the evil eye; it is as if someone has put a spell on them.
3.mean: Paul makes two arguments. The first is from experience. When Christ crucified was ‘clearly portrayed’ before them, did they receive the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith? They received the Spirit before anyone told them about circumcision. So having begun by the Spirit, why try to be finished off by the flesh? The second is from Scripture. ‘Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness’ (Genesis 15:6). This was said of Abraham before he was circumcised (Genesis 17), and centuries before Sinai. So the true children of Abraham are those who believe, and Scripture ‘foresaw’ that God would justify Gentiles by faith. The promise ‘all nations will be blessed through you’ was the gospel announced in advance.
3.big: The Galatians’ own experience of the Spirit, and Abraham’s own story, both show that God accepts people through faith.

src.l: D. Mangum & D. R. Brown, Galatians, Logos Research Commentaries (Lexham), surveying Betz, Bruce, Dunn, George, Hays, Longenecker, Martyn, Schreiner and others

3.ctx: Paul now argues from the law itself, quoting Deuteronomy 27:26, Habakkuk 2:4, Leviticus 18:5 and Deuteronomy 21:23.
3.mean: This is where Paul makes plain why the law cannot save. ‘All who rely on works of the law are under a curse’, because the law itself says, ‘Cursed is everyone who does not continue to do everything written in the Book of the Law’. The unstated step is that no one does everything. The law demands complete obedience, and everyone falls short. Meanwhile Scripture names another way: ‘The righteous will live by faith’. The law works on a different principle, ‘The man who does these things will live by them’. Then comes the answer. ‘Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us’, since the law says, ‘Cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree’. Crucifixion was the most shameful of deaths, and to a Jewish mind a crucified man looked cursed by God. Paul says that is exactly what happened, but the curse was ours. The result is that Abraham’s blessing reaches the Gentiles, and we receive the promised Spirit through faith.
3.big: Christ took the law’s curse on himself so that its blessing could reach those who believe.
3.diff: How does Christ ‘becoming a curse for us’? Reformed and many evangelical scholars, such as Schreiner, read it as substitution: Christ bore in our place the penalty our law-breaking deserved (the doctrine often called penal substitution). Longenecker speaks of an ‘exchange’: Christ takes our curse and we receive his blessing. Dunn reads it representatively: Christ took the place of the covenant-breaker outside the covenant, opening the blessing to Gentiles. Most Arminian theologians also hold that Christ died in our place, while some prefer to describe it in other ways, for example as Christ satisfying God’s moral government. All agree that Christ’s death is the means by which the curse is removed.

3.ctx: Paul answers the obvious question: if God’s promise to Abraham came first, what was the law for? He uses the picture of a will, which cannot be changed once it is ratified.
3.mean: The law came 430 years after the promise, so it cannot cancel or add conditions to it. The inheritance comes by promise, not by law. Paul notes that the promise was to Abraham’s ‘seed’, singular, which he applies to Christ, the one true offspring in whom all believers share. So why the law? ‘It was added because of transgressions, until the arrival of the seed to whom the promise referred.’ Is the law then against the promises? ‘Certainly not!’ But no law could give life. Instead ‘the Scripture pronounces all things confined by sin’, so that the promise would be given through faith. The law was our paidagōgos, ‘guardian’: in Greek and Roman households, a trusted slave who escorted and disciplined a boy until he came of age. Now that faith has come, we are no longer under the guardian.
3.big: The law was never a rival way to God’s blessing; it was a temporary guardian that exposed sin and kept God’s people until Christ came.
3.diff: ‘Added because of transgressions’ may mean that the law was given to restrain sin, or to expose it as law-breaking (compare Romans 5:20; 7:7). Reformed and Lutheran theology has long taught that one use of the law is to convict of sin and drive people to Christ. The mention of angels and a mediator (verses 19–20) is among the most obscure lines in Paul. The mediator is almost certainly Moses, and the angels reflect a Jewish tradition also found in Acts 7:53 and Hebrews 2:2. The point seems to be that the law came to Israel at one remove, while the promise came from God directly. The ‘430 years’ follows Exodus 12:40.

3.ctx: The conclusion of the argument begun in 3:1. Baptism, the public sign of entering the church, is used as shorthand for belonging to Christ.
3.mean: Everyone who is in Christ is a son of God through faith. ‘Sons’ here is legal language for heirs, and it includes daughters. All who were baptised into Christ have ‘clothed yourselves with Christ’. So ‘there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus’. These were the three great divisions of the ancient world. In Christ none of them decides who belongs or who inherits. And if you belong to Christ, the one Seed, you are Abraham’s seed and heirs according to the promise. Gentiles do not need circumcision to become Abraham’s children; they already are, in Christ.
3.big: In Christ every believer shares equally in God’s family and inheritance, whatever their background.
3.diff: Verse 28 is often cited in debates about men and women in church leadership. Complementarian scholars, such as Schreiner, read it as about equal standing and inheritance before God, not the removal of every distinction, since Paul elsewhere still addresses men and women, slaves and masters, separately. Egalitarian scholars see it as having wider implications for roles in church life. In context, the verse’s first point is that no one has a lesser place in God’s family. How baptism relates to faith here (verse 27) is read differently too. For Catholic, Orthodox and Lutheran Christians, baptism is a means through which God unites a person to Christ. For most Reformed and Baptist Christians it is the God-given sign and seal of a union received by faith.

4.ctx: Paul continues the picture of an heir who, while still a child, is no better off than a slave. He is under guardians until the date his father has set.
4.mean: Before Christ, Paul says, ‘we were enslaved under the basic principles of the world’. ‘But when the time had fully come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law, that we might receive our adoption as sons.’ Each phrase counts. The Son was sent: he existed with the Father before he was born. He was born of a woman: truly human. He was born under the law: a real Jew who kept the law we broke. He came at the time God chose. Christians have long read verse 4 as holding together Christ’s divinity and his full humanity (see the note on Mark 4:35). Then God ‘sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying out, “Abba, Father!”’ Abba is the Aramaic word Jesus himself used in prayer (Mark 14:36). The Father sends the Son and the Son’s Spirit, so believers share in Jesus’ own relationship with the Father. So ‘you are no longer a slave, but a son; and since you are a son, you are also an heir through God’.
4.big: God sent both his Son and his Spirit so that believers would be not slaves but children, able to call God ‘Father’.
4.diff: ‘The Spirit of his Son’ (verse 6) is one of the texts Western churches, Catholic and Protestant alike, have cited for teaching that the Spirit proceeds from the Father ‘and the Son’ (the filioque, added to the Western form of the Nicene Creed). The Eastern Orthodox churches hold that the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, and read this verse as describing the Spirit’s being sent to believers, not his eternal origin. Both sides confess the full deity of the Spirit. ‘Basic principles’ (Greek stoicheia; footnote: ‘elemental forces’) is debated. It may mean elementary religious rules, the physical elements, or spiritual powers. Paul applies it both to life under the law and to pagan religion (verse 9), which is part of his point.

4.ctx: Before they became Christians, the Galatians worshipped pagan gods. Paul now fears they are slipping back into a similar slavery by taking up the law’s calendar of special days.
4.mean: Once they did not know God and were slaves ‘to those who by nature are not gods’. Now they know God, ‘or rather are known by God’. Paul corrects himself, because their relationship began with God knowing them. So how can they turn back to ‘weak and worthless principles’, observing ‘days and months and seasons and years’? He fears his work among them has been wasted. Then Paul turns personal. He first preached to them because of an illness. They did not despise his condition but welcomed him ‘as if I were an angel of God’; they would have torn out their own eyes for him. Has he now become their enemy by telling the truth? The other teachers court them to win them over for themselves. Paul feels like a mother in labour again ‘until Christ is formed in you’.
4.big: Going back to rules as the way to stand before God is a return to slavery, not progress; the goal is Christ formed in us.
4.diff: Paul does not name his illness. Because of the eyes in verse 15 and the ‘large letters’ of 6:11, some have suggested an eye condition, but this is guesswork, and many scholars (Betz, Dunn) read 6:11 differently. Paul’s warning about ‘days and months’ concerns keeping them as a requirement for acceptance with God (compare Romans 14:5–6), not Christians marking special days in themselves.

4.ctx: Paul turns his opponents’ own ground, the law and the story of Abraham, against them. He invites those who want to be under the law to listen to what the law (here meaning the books of Moses) actually says.
4.mean: Abraham had two sons. Ishmael was born to the slave woman Hagar ‘according to the flesh’, by ordinary human means when Abraham and Sarah tried to bring about God’s promise themselves. Isaac was born to the free woman Sarah ‘through the promise’, by God’s miraculous action (Genesis 16–21). Paul says he is reading the story figuratively. The two women stand for two covenants. Hagar stands for Mount Sinai and ‘the present-day Jerusalem’, in slavery. Sarah stands for ‘the Jerusalem above’, which is free and is our mother. Isaiah 54:1 promised that the barren woman would have more children than the married one. Believers, like Isaac, are children of promise. And as Ishmael mocked Isaac, so now those born of the flesh pressure those born of the Spirit. Scripture’s answer is: ‘Expel the slave woman and her son.’ For the Galatians, that means sending away the teaching that would put them back into slavery.
4.big: Those who rely on the law for acceptance are children of slavery; those who trust God’s promise are children of freedom.
4.diff: Paul uses the verb allēgoreō, ‘to speak allegorically’ (verse 24). Scholars debate whether this is allegory in the later sense, where details stand for hidden ideas, or typology, a pattern repeated in history. Many, including Betz and Schreiner, see a mixture of the two. Philo of Alexandria also allegorised this story, but very differently. Some readers today worry about how the passage could be turned against Jewish people. In context, Paul’s target is teachers within the church who required Gentile believers to take on the law, not Jewish people as such (compare Romans 9:1–5; 11:1).

5.ctx: The turn from argument to practice. ‘Freedom’ is the key word of the rest of the letter.
5.mean: ‘It is for freedom that Christ has set us free. Stand firm, then, and do not be encumbered once more by a yoke of slavery.’ Paul spells out what accepting circumcision as a requirement would mean. Christ would be of no value to them. They would be obliged to keep the whole law. They would be ‘severed from Christ’ and ‘fallen away from grace’. You cannot rely on Christ and on your own law-keeping at the same time; one excludes the other. Instead, ‘by faith we eagerly await through the Spirit the hope of righteousness’. In Christ neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, what matters is ‘faith, expressing itself through love’. Saving faith is never idle. It works itself out in love, though love is its fruit, not its foundation. Paul’s wish that the agitators would ‘emasculate themselves’ (verse 12) is deliberately coarse. If cutting the flesh saves, let them go all the way.
5.big: To rely on the law for acceptance is to let go of grace; the faith that saves shows itself in love.
5.diff: Christians differ over ‘you have fallen away from grace’ (verse 4). Reformed theology holds that those truly united to Christ will be kept by God to the end (Westminster Confession 17.1). It reads the verse as describing people who abandon the way of grace for the way of law, which shows they were never resting on Christ, or as a real warning God uses to keep his people. Arminian theology takes it as describing a real possibility that a true believer can turn away and be lost. John Wesley argued this in Serious Thoughts upon the Perseverance of the Saints. The original Arminian articles of 1610 left the question open. Catholic teaching holds that grace can be lost through grave sin and restored through repentance and the sacrament of penance (Trent, Session 6, ch. 14). All agree the verse is a serious warning against trusting anything besides Christ.

5.ctx: Having warned against the law, Paul now warns against the opposite mistake: treating freedom as permission to indulge the flesh (5:13).
5.mean: ‘Walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh.’ ‘Flesh’ here does not mean the body. It means human nature turned in on itself and away from God. Flesh and Spirit are at war, so that you do not do what you want. Paul lists ‘the acts of the flesh’: sexual sin, idolatry and sorcery, then a long run of community-wrecking sins (hatred, discord, jealousy, rage, rivalries, divisions, factions, envy), and finally drunkenness and carousing. He warns that those who live like this ‘will not inherit the kingdom of God’. Against these he sets the ‘fruit of the Spirit’: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control. ‘Against such things there is no law.’ The law demanded this character but could not produce it; the Spirit grows it. Those who belong to Christ ‘have crucified the flesh’, so ‘let us walk in step with the Spirit’.
5.big: The Spirit produces in believers the character the law demanded but could not create.
5.diff: ‘Fruit’ is singular: one harvest with nine aspects, not a menu of separate gifts. Luther and others noted that Paul says ‘fruit’ rather than ‘works’ of the Spirit, because it is grown, not manufactured. How the struggle in verse 17 relates to Romans 7 is debated. Reformed interpreters generally see an ongoing tension in every Christian life, in which the Spirit is the stronger. Wesleyan theology also expects real, sometimes decisive, growth in holiness in this life (‘entire sanctification’), while agreeing that believers are never beyond the need of grace.

6.mean: If someone is caught in a sin, ‘you who are spiritual’ (those led by the Spirit, not a spiritual elite) should restore him gently, watching yourselves in case you are tempted too. ‘Restore’ is the word used for mending nets or setting a bone. ‘Carry one another’s burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ.’ The law of Christ is the life of self-giving love Christ himself lived (compare 5:14; John 13:34). No one should think himself something; each should test his own work, ‘for each one should carry his own load’. Those taught the word should share good things with their teachers. Then a solemn principle: ‘God is not to be mocked. Whatever a man sows, he will reap in return.’ Sow to the flesh and reap decay; sow to the Spirit and reap eternal life. ‘Let us not grow weary in well-doing’, doing good to everyone, ‘especially to the family of faith’.
6.big: The freedom of the gospel is lived out in gentle restoration, shared burdens and persistent good.
6.diff: Verses 2 and 5 look contradictory: bear one another’s burdens, yet each carries his own load. Paul uses two different Greek words. The ‘burdens’ of verse 2 (barē) are heavy troubles we should share. The ‘load’ of verse 5 (phortion) is the ordinary responsibility each person answers to God for. ‘Sowing to the Spirit’ (verse 8) does not mean earning eternal life. Paul has spent the whole letter denying that. It describes the direction of a life that the Spirit is leading.

6.ctx: Letters were usually written by a secretary (compare Romans 16:22). Here Paul takes the pen to write the ending himself, as authors often did to authenticate a letter.
6.mean: ‘See what large letters I am using to write to you with my own hand!’ Whatever the reason for the size, it underlines what follows. The agitators want to ‘make a good impression outwardly’. They push circumcision to avoid persecution for the cross, and they do not keep the law themselves; they want to boast about the Galatians’ flesh. Paul will boast only ‘in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world’. Neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything; what counts is ‘a new creation’. Peace and mercy rest on all who walk by this rule. No one should trouble him further, because he bears on his body ‘the marks of Jesus’, almost certainly the scars of beatings and stoning (compare Acts 14:19; 2 Corinthians 11:23–25). Unlike the agitators, he has suffered for the cross.
6.big: The only thing worth boasting in is the cross, because through it God makes a new creation.
6.diff: Who is ‘the Israel of God’ (verse 16)? The Greek kai can mean ‘and’ or ‘even’, and the BSB’s ‘even’ reflects one view. Many interpreters, including most in the Reformed tradition, take Paul to mean the whole church of Jewish and Gentile believers: ‘peace on all who walk by this rule, that is, on the Israel of God’. Others read ‘and on the Israel of God’ as a second group: Jewish believers in particular, or the Jewish people whom God will yet show mercy to (compare Romans 11:26). Moo and Longenecker are among the commentators who set out the arguments in detail. The question affects how Christians understand the relationship between Israel and the church. Some suggest the large letters point to poor eyesight (compare 4:15); many commentators, such as Betz, Dunn and Martyn, take them simply as emphasis, like underlining.
